utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Court deputy, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President, Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, how long have you known Dragan Jokic? A: Mr. McCloskey, I first met Mr. Jokic sometime around the 15th of June, 1992. That's when I saw him first, and that's when we got to know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you briefly describe your professional relationship.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I came to the Zvornik Brigade on the 1st of December, 1992, up until that time, Major Jokic was chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade. I took over that duty from him, and he went to become the chief of the engineers of the Zvornik Brigade, to take up that post. So along those lines, we had a professional relationship, until in 1995 - the beginning of May, in fact, 1995 - I started to take over the duty of -- or rather, acting commander of the brigade. I became that. And when I -- to all intents and purposes became commander of the brigade, he was assigned elsewhere to take up another post. Of course, during certain periods when I was acting in for the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, the relationship was that I was the commander and he was still chief of the engineers Brigade. So we had this professional relationship going. And I think that our cooperation was correct and proper. Nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have any friendship outside of the professional relationships or outside the military sphere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so, no. Mostly it was a professional relationship, proper, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Up until this period of 1995, you spoke to -- had there been any major problems or issues between you in the professional relationship?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but, as you know, it was a difficult period. There was a war on. We encountered various problems. So there would always be some professional disagreement, as you would have anywhere else, but nothing specific or important. We worked during difficult times. We had difficult tasks to do. So of course there would be some tension and friction from time to time, but nothing of any significance; at least, that's how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about post-war? Can you describe your professional relationship post-war, post-1995, I should say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps similar to what I've already described. We could say that we had a certain amount of friction - I don't know if I'm using the right word - sometime in 1998, when, due to certain problems that arose in the unit, and I was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade already at that time, and Mr. Jokic performed the function of chief of the operations sector, there was a problem that cropped up with respect to some explosive device, which SFOR had uncovered, and after that we conducted some internal investigations of our own, and at one point Mr. Jokic accused me of perhaps working for SFOR. So that was a major issue between us. Afterwards, I asked to report to the Corps Commander, and I asked the commander to take steps to either take him away from the command or myself, because we could no longer work together. I think it was in the summer of 1998 -- to have one of us transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the summer of 1998, did the investigation into Srebrenica play any role in the tension between you and Mr. Jokic at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after -- well, what did -- when you recommended to the commander not to work with -- not to have Mr. Jokic work with you any more, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, the Corps Commander decided to transfer Jokic to the command of the 5th Corps at Sokolac, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know the other accused in this case, Mr. Vidoje Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Blagojevic, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, during that same period of time, as with Mr. Jokic, in mid-June sometime, when I first arrived in Zvornik, or rather, the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him less well. That is to say, I knew Mr. Blagojevic less well. We would see each other less frequently. But I think he was a quiet man. That's the impression he gave me - fairly introverted. He went about his own business. That's how I saw him. We didn't actually see each other very often. We worked at different headquarters in different commands, so we wouldn't come across each other that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was he commander of the Zvornik Brigade early on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, precisely in June. That's when he was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. I don't know for how long. A relatively short period of time. If I remember correctly, he was taken ill and he went off on sick leave to undergo treatment somewhere. And then I left Zvornik after that, that is to say on the 1st of December that same year. When I came back he wasn't there. I didn't find him there any more. But later on as he worked in the command of the Drina Corps, we would come across each other from time to time on our various assignments. Our paths would cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any troubles or problems between you two, Mr. Blagojevic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you've described, you've had an opportunity to command a VRS brigade. I know courses are given on command, so this is somewhat of an unfair question, but could you, for the Court, describe to us the essence of command, the main responsibilities of command as you see it. Take your time and organise your thoughts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander is the most responsible individual, and when I say commander, I mean brigade commander. He is the most responsible person in a brigade. He has the exclusive right of commanding and issuing orders to all the subordinates in the brigade. So to the command, parts of the command, and also subordinate units, as well as units that might perhaps be at some point attached to it. And it is from these rights that he enjoys, as commander, he assigns tasks to units and individuals, and he has full responsibility, takes full responsibility for everything that happens within his units and in the area of defence or area of responsibility of that particular unit. The tasks of a brigade commander are -- and his duties are fairly broad in scope and highly complex. In addition to issuing assignments to his subordinates, he also does certain other basic things, to make it simple: He commands and issues orders; he issues guidelines for all the planning that goes on; he controls and sees whether the tasks issued are being carried out and whether the plans are being put into practice; he takes the necessary steps and measures to ensure that the orders issued are being carried out; he sees to the disciplinary side and stimulates soldiers, as well as sanctioning them if they have not been carried out; and he has reports from the subordinates and reports to his superiors. Of course, the commander does not do all these things alone. He has the staff in the command at his disposal to assist him. At this juncture, I should like to emphasise that the commander can delegate his rights of command to somebody, whether that be the Chief of Staff or one of his assistants or another chief of another sector. However, that does not free him of his responsibilities. He continues to be responsible for what any one of these subordinates does, for all their acts, whether they be positive or negative. He takes full responsibility, although he has delegated part of his rights to command to that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are a commander's responsibilities in enforcing the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To see that they are adhered to and implemented, that the Geneva Conventions are observed and put into practice, and to ensure that his subordinates, the chiefs of the various units, go about putting the conventions into practice. And they stem from the commanders' duties. So the officer who is in command, that is one level, and all the other levels, all the other officers in command, commanding officers of an army, must observe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How does that extend to the care of prisoners in custody in his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the duty of one and all to act in conformity with the Geneva Conventions, to ensure that the prisoners have the necessary protection, to safeguard their lives, to create conditions as prescribed by the conventions for accommodation, food, and medical care and protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your training to become a JNA officer, did you receive training in the Geneva Conventions and the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And if I remember correctly, that was in the first year of military academy. I don't remember the semester we did this in, but we had an examination on law, including international war law. We had a course on that, and then sat for our examinations. So my answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are a commander's responsibilities related to knowing what is going on around him in his zone of responsibility and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such responsibilities do exist. Quite simply, for a commander to be able to make decisions of any kind, he is duty-bound to take measures and steps to acquaint himself with what is going on in his own unit, what is happening in his -- with his next-door neighbours, both in the enemy camp and in the area of responsibility of his own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about superior commands that come to his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would include superior commands. They are duty-bound to see that all information and intelligence relevant to its subordinate units should be divulged to the subordinate commander so that he be kept abreast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what does a brigade commander have in order for him to become acquainted with and learn about what's going on around him, all the things you've described? What facilities does he have to look to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander, in my view, in order to be able to have the necessary information to command the area around him, he has the following resources: First of all, he has the corresponding organs in the brigade command, and when I say that, I mean first and foremost the security organs and intelligence organs, and these are duty-bound to keep him informed, each within the frameworks of their field of action. Next we have information coming to him from the Superior Command and different individuals there, both civilians or MUP personnel in the area of responsibility of his particular unit. And finally, everything else he considers to be necessary in order to take the necessary steps to ensure that he is kept informed and has all the information before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where does the duty officer fit into this communication link with the commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the duty officer has an important role to play. The duty officer has the role of ensuring continuity of command at all times. So it is the responsibility of the duty officer to inform the commander about events, to convey all relevant information to him, either from a superior or from the duty officer of the Drina Corps, or from duty officers from subordinate units. So the duty officer, operative duty officer, keeps his commander informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are there any records kept daily that a commander can review to find out what's going on in his unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the duty officer, operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Among any records that the commander has access to, what records does the commander have access to in his brigade command to help him figure out what's going on, say if he's been gone a while and comes back?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander can ask to see and gain insight into most of the documents that are being kept and recorded in his unit. Perhaps there are a few documents that the security officer has which might not be given to the brigade commander, but otherwise everything else would be made accessible to him, regardless of whether they're being kept by the operations duty officer or other individuals in the brigade's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What in particular - records - are there kept in the offices of the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about July 1995, then the operations duty officer would keep the following records: First, a logbook of the operations duty officer of the brigade, the shift book, where the handover of duty is recorded; then another work logbook; and then something else that we called files, storing combat reports, regular daily combat reports sent out to the Drina Corps; and then there was another book, or log, of recruits, recording recruits passing through the garrison. So that, for the most part, would be the written material that the operations duty officer of the brigade would keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll go over some of those logs a little bit later. But what was your situation in the months leading up to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of 1995, I was occupying my regular duties as Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade. On the 16th of April, 1995, I was wounded in my left leg, and so had to undergo treatment, post operative treatment as well. On the 1st of July, 1995, I returned to take up my duties as Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and once the units of the Zvornik Brigade had left and gone to Srebrenica on the 4th of July, automatically, because the commander had left with part of the units to the Srebrenica area, I became deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade. This was an automatic process. So until the commander returned, or more exactly the 15th of July, sometime around noon, I performed the functions of deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade and was to all intents and purpose it's in command of parts of the unit of the Zvornik Brigade which were in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade, in the area of Zvornik, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was your wound received in combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, during combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While you were leading your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first find out about the operation to attack the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I first found out about it on the 29th of June, in the evening. The commander and another officer came to see me at my house, because I was on sick leave. They asked that I interrupt my sick leave and return to the command of the brigade. Since certain preparations were being conducted for part of the units to move towards Srebrenica. So that's when I heard it for the first time, by way of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us the preparations that were conducted by the Zvornik Brigade in which troops actually went out to take part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preparations of the Zvornik Brigade for the Srebrenica operation, or, as it was called in the military plans, Krivaja 95, began intensively during the 2nd of July, 1995. That's when we -- or rather, the Zvornik Brigade, was given a preparatory order from the Drina Corps command, intimating the operation, and then another order reached us, which defined in more specific terms and details the duties and obligations of the Zvornik Brigade. And the commander took the decision and afterwards an order was written out regulating the duties of the Zvornik Brigade itself. The unit which was being prepared to go to Srebrenica was set up on the basis of a decision by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic. A Combat Group was set up. It had a command and two battalions. That's what it consisted of. The first battalion, if I can call it that, was made up of the Podrinje attachment, establishment-wise, the Wolves, and the second unit was composed of all -- or rather, a part of the battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, one intervention platoon was taken from all the battalions except from the 5th Battalion. And those men set up two companies. The commander of a unit established in this way was Lieutenant Stanojevic, the commander of the first battalion. The commander of this whole composition from the Zvornik Brigade was Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, our commander, and his deputy, in addition to his regular duties, was the commander of the Wolves, Captain First Class Milan Jolovic. That in brief is what the establishment looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was Jolovic's nickname?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first learn that the Srebrenica enclave fell?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first learnt of the fall of Srebrenica on the 11th, in the afternoon, the 11th of July, 1995, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what information did you receive, if any, on the 12th of July relating to what was happening in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the information media and also through various reports and information from the Superior Command, we did know roughly what was going on in Potocari. So we had the information media. They carried information about the evacuation, and we were also ordered to send some transport vehicles, that is to say, a few buses and trucks. So that's it, generally speaking. So roughly, we did know what was happening with respect to the evacuation of the population. We didn't know anything about the details, but roughly speaking we did know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know what the buses and trucks that you sent down from your area were to be used for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew, for transporting the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At that point, on the 12th, did you know anything about -- the able-bodied men were being separated from the civilian population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could take a short moment and we're going to set up a map to help visualise all this, Mr. President. This is Exhibit 20.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, before we get to this map, aside from the basic information about Potocari that you were aware of on the 12th, did you receive any information about the Muslim 28th Division and the whereabouts of the soldiers from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received the first information about this on the morning of the 12th, not before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning hours, perhaps around 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what information did you receive, you yourself, and when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally received my first information from our group that was in Gucovo. They had intercepted somewhere some radio communications from people from the column of the 28th Division, and at first we did not know what this was about and where this unit was. Perhaps an hour went by, until we identified the forces concerned and roughly where they could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just tell us what you thought at that point the forces were and where they were.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we identified this, we thought that these were parts of the 28th Division, not the entire unit. After my telephone conversation with the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade - or rather, this unit had previously been our 8th Battalion a year before that - he informed me that parts of the 28th Division were passing between his area near Buljin and the Milici Brigade. My information was that these were parts of the unit, and groups that made up a column that consisted of a maximum of 1.500 men, and the column was not all in one piece, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time did you have this phone call with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was around 7.00 in the morning on the 12th, approximately. Sometime before I immediately transferred this information to the command of the Drina Corps -- transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander that you spoke to from the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radika Petrovic, Captain First Class Radika Petrovic. I talked to his duty officer in the battalion, because he was already at the positions facing those groups that were passing by. So I did not speak to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us why you were concerned? It may seem obvious, but could you explain.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had to be -- this had to do with our neighbour, to put it in civilian terms, the neighbouring brigade, and it was my duty to follow what was going on at my next-door neighbour's so to speak, from a combat point of view. That is one thing. Another thing is that for a long period of time, to be precise, from mid-1993, we had had experience with these various groups, either from the area of the 28th Division of Srebrenica or the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Tuzla. They were passing through the area of responsibility of our brigade, the Zvornik Brigade. And I assumed that they would take one of the customary corridors, the three or four that were customary, and that they would continue to pass there and that sooner or later they would come and threaten the positions of our brigade, the Zvornik Brigade. Hence my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you show us with that laser pointer the customary corridor you're referring to. If you can figure out how to work that thing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Srebrenica, and I think that what is shown on this map, if I understand this correctly, these are the positions that denote the enclave. The positions of our units were on one side and on the other side, on the inner side of the enclave, the positions of the units of the 28th Division. Somewhere around here was the position of the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, or rather, our former 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. Your question had to do with the customary corridors of the area of the Zvornik Brigade. They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, and I -- just for the record, I want to say: You said your troops -- and you pointed to the area where they were, and this was on the map just north of the village of Jaglici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you tell us a location, if you could use a reference that's on that map so that later, when someone reads the record of this, they will understand roughly the area we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do that. So this is the town of Zvornik. The position of the Zvornik Brigade, the positions of the Zvornik Brigade were at the north. One will be able to find on the map the facility called Tursan Brdo and Konjski Put, or rather, these are features on the map. Towards the left, towards the left wing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't need to be too detailed. I will provide you with a more detailed map later.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the village of Memici on the left, near the Spreca River. This is a very big map, but roughly that's where this is. The corridors you referred to were here, between the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade to the north of the village of Jaglici, and the next unit that was one infantry battalion from the Milici Light Infantry Brigade at Ravni Buljin. There was an area that was never taken by units. Roughly it covered perhaps 800 metres to one kilometre. It had been mined. And the groups that went to and from Srebrenica usually used that. They usually go out that way and then they would move along these mountain roads, abandoned roads, through this area, this broad area of Cerska, then they would cross to the area behind Zvornik, the area of Kamenica; from there, they usually went in the following directions: One direction was from Kamenica, say from this village, Cancari, up across Crni Vrh, and then up here towards Paljkovica and Nezuk. That was one direction. The other was from the village of Cancari, they would go here towards Memici this side of the tunnel, through the Pretanska [phoen] hill and then they would enter the area of Kalesija. Those are the two directions relevant to the Zvornik Brigade, from Cancari there was yet another route towards Paprace, towards this mountainous area here. I've forgotten the exact names of the villages there. But on this map that's roughly the area I'm referring to. This was a corridor that we knew about, one that was a bit further away from us and that went from Srebrenica across the Han Pijesak forests and then towards Kladanj, around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what other information you learned on the 12th about the -- specifically about the Muslims, and also about -- did you become aware of what VRS units dealing with them in this area where they began north of Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. McCloskey. When you say the Muslims, are you referring to the column of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the day progressed, on the 12th, I was receiving more and more information about this problem that I thought was relevant or even dangerous for the unit that I was in then. We received a series of information from this radio intercept group of ours, Premier, then the information that the Superior Command gave us, and also part of the information that came from the MUP. Then further on, I myself took some measures that were reflected in the following: I sent my assistant commander for intelligence affairs, captain Vukotic, to this battalion, in Sekovici, the Kajica village, where its command was, and I asked him to seek information there directly with regard to this specific information. So during the second half of the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you just tell us where Kajica is in relation to Bratunac or Kravica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kravica along the road towards Bratunac, perhaps at this curve here, if I remember correctly. So from Kravica along this asphalt road towards Bratunac, perhaps 500 metres up to one kilometre. I cannot remember exactly - there was a village that was called Kajica. And in this village of Kajica was the commander of the 4th Battalion. And I've already described its positions there from Ravni Buljin and further on towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, on the 12th, I dealt with other matters, or to be more precise, I was in Memici at our 7th Battalion because 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already started attacking. And when I returned in the afternoon, the intelligence officer was - I mean, when I returned to the brigade command, to be quite precise - this intelligence officer had already returned from Kajica from the command there, and from him I heard this information, roughly what was going on over there, namely, that parts of the units of the 28th Division were carrying out a penetration and evacuation through this space and that practically the entire area was overwhelmed by people from this column, and that there was a second blockade in front of the column of the 28th Division, and that this was placed already in part on this road here, between Kravica and Konjevic Polje, to put it roughly, and Nova Kasaba where the asphalt road is, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what VRS units were taking part in this blockade at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, in that area the following units, VRS units, were there: One battalion of the Protection Regiment that was precisely here in Kasaba; then part of the units of the 55th engineering battalion from the Drina Corps that was otherwise located here in Konjevic Polje. Although I think that it should be pointed out that they had very few men and that they could only take care of themselves. But since they were there, it can be said that they constituted a unit that was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who else did you know about was looking after that area besides those two units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also there were the forces of the Zvornik MUP, a company, and there was another company that was getting ready to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Another company from where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these companies are of the Zvornik centre of the security service. I could not say exactly where they got them from, but we called them the blue police. These are special units of the police that were trained for combat, and they were able to engage in combat with the enemy. And they were commanded by the Zvornik security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was -- would have been their commander at the Zvornik security centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the security centre was Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel then, Dragomir Vasic. Mane Djuric was his deputy. Colonel Vasic was absent probably up there in the area of Bratunac or Srebrenica - I don't know exactly where. On that day, on the 12th, that is, I spoke to Lieutenant Colonel Djuric a few times. He was in Zvornik and we talked over the telephone precisely about these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Court has heard about the special police forces of Ljubisa Borovcanin. Can you distinguish how they are different from the forces that you've just described under the command of Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try, Mr. McCloskey. My knowledge is probably very modest in this area. But to the best of my understanding, at the level of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, there was a special unit that was called the brigade of the special police of Republika Srpska. Its commander was -- I don't know what his rank was, but his name was Goran Saric. Perhaps he was a colonel. His deputy was Mr. Borovcanin, who you mentioned just now, and he was also Chief of Staff. This was a unit at the level of the MUP of Republika Srpska and it consisted of several detachments. I think seven at the time, perhaps eight. So in July 1995, that's the way it was. As opposed to that, every centre of security of the MUP, including the Zvornik centre, had a unit that was equipped and trained from amongst its regular ranks. This unit was established for specific tasks, combat operations, and they were called special police forces. So if I understood this correctly, these were ordinary policemen who, during their regular work hours, so to speak, dealt with the maintenance of law and order in their regular work. But if necessary, they would set up this special unit of the police. They would wear military uniforms. They had standard military weapons, light weapons, for the most part. And they were used in combat, just like military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could just describe briefly, if you could, the knowledge you gained from mid-July 12, midday, up until, say, midday on the 13th. If you could just outline for us what you learned and what you were doing. But just in an outline format. We don't need all the real detail at this point.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean generally speaking or are you referring to something specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean -- well, generally. Let me ask one specific question before we get there. Did you send any troops down to the area of Konjevic Polje on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Zvornik Brigade sent to Konjevic Polje on the 12th one squad or a half squad of traffic police, at the intersection there, in order to regulate traffic there. We received written orders from the Drina Corps to that effect, and we acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many men was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, five or six probably. They could all fit into one car and they simply left. I really can't remember all the details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So again, if you could generally describe the events as you learned them from midday on the 12th until midday on the 13th. Just give us an overview.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon of the 12th, I tried to clarify matters for myself and for the unit, to see what was going on south of us, in the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac, with this column of the 28th Division. In the afternoon of the 12th, we received one or two intelligence reports, either from the command of the Drina Corps or the Main Staff, and this had to do with the information received from prisoners of war who were interrogated and then this had to do with the possible future movement of the 28th Division. Also I received information after my conversation with Mr. Mane Djuric in the afternoon of the 12th. He had been in Vlasenica and he had toured his units in Konjevic Polje. And he acquainted me in quite a bit of detail as to what was going on there and what the problems were and what should be done. As for this information I received from him, later on I conveyed them to the operations duty officer of the command of the Drina Corps. I received commander -- information from Commander Vukovic, my intelligence officer, that is to say the intelligence officer of the brigade. I've already referred to this a while ago, so I don't have to go into all of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you're speaking a little quickly. I can tell the interpreter is having to -- so if you could slow down a bit, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In the early evening of the 12th, we had information that measures were being taken to block this column of the 28th Division on the mentioned road, that is to say, Kravica, Nova Kasaba, Milici. And by then, parts of these units, smaller groups, as our intelligence said then, managed to reach this other area of Glogova and Cerska by then. So I received a task to take all necessary measures in order to protect the elements of combat deployment of the brigade. These villages too in the territory of Zvornik that had been populated. So this is roughly the information I had in the early evening of the 12th. The initial information was that this was about 150 men who managed to break through, and the other piece of information referred to a unit of 300 men divided into several groups, who had come to that area which was right behind us, the Zvornik Brigade. And sometime late during the night, perhaps exactly at midnight, between the 12th and 13th, I personally went with a group of our units to this area here, right above Zvornik, to the south of -- or rather, to the north of the village of Liplje. And I organised an ambush, because I expected that that would be the place where these groups would pass. And that is where we were on the morning of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you again briefly describe what information you were getting on the 13th and what you did. But very generally and in an outline format.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 13th, we were up there, but we didn't find anything out. We searched the area, and sometime after noon, via the devices I was told to go back to Zvornik, that there were no major forces in our area. So I left part of the troops up there at Snagovo, and the rest returned to Zvornik. Upon my arrival at headquarters, brigade headquarters, I was informed that the column had been stopped on the road just mentioned, from Kravica, Konjevic Polje, to Milici, and that there were no major troops, that just smaller groups had managed to break through into our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time was that that you went back to the brigade headquarters and received that information on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to speak about the time exactly, but it was sometime after noon, probably, after midday. Not too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who had told you to go back to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to go back to the brigade was taken by myself. I made the decision, based on the information I received by radio to the effect that the road to Konjevic Polje -- that an ambush had been set up there and that there were no major forces there. So it was my assessment that there was no need for me to be up there any more and that the units I left up there would succeed in dealing with the small groups that might be passing along that way. So I made the decision to return on the basis of the information I received from the duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know in the afternoon of the 13th who that duty officer was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer on the 13th was captain Sreten Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so after receiving that information, can you just continue. What else sort of generally happened on the day of the 13th and what information did you receive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon after my arrival, the intercept groups informed us once again that they were hearing a lot of traffic again, and they located this in the area stretching from Cerska towards Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've mentioned Kamenica a couple of times. Can you describe where it is in relation to villages we can see on this map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kamenica is a broader area encompassing the following villages: Liplje, probably Hodzici, towards Cancari. That's where Kamenica is, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a broad area comprising several villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if you could continue.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, this was a period of time when I was receiving a series of contradictory information. What the Superior Command, that is to say, the Drina Corps command, claimed was that there were no significant forces crossing into the rear of us. However, from the intercept groups conducting interception, we began receiving more and more information to the opposite, that there was a big column, and this column of the 28th Division, it seems that their radio discipline was flagging and they began to speak about numbers themselves. So our intercept centre learnt that the number was 1.000 to 1.500 people in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, broadly, what did you do that afternoon, evening, on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the information received, I made the decision to strengthen the units that had stayed up there in providing the ambush. I decided to organise a provisional unit, grouping squad and platoon from the units at my disposal, and so was able to form a unit which had the strength of a company. And Captain Milan Maric from the operations sector, was made commander, and I sent them up there. Another remaining platoon from the military police company which had not been deployed at that time I sent to the ambush at Siroki Put and they were there to do reconnaissance work of the Drinjaca River canyon by the village of Glodi roughly, where there were two bridges, and it was my assessment that if the column were to pass by in the direction we expected it to move that they would probably make use of those two bridges. And this is roughly the area where the village of Siroki Put is located from where they could observe the bridges. So setting up an ambush of this kind by the military police platoon at Siroki Put and the other one at Dzafin Kamen, another military platoon, and the rest of the ambush above the village of Liplje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you use any units or any people from the engineering company for this group?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A moment ago, when I said I set up a mixed company, the composition of that mixed company was roughly the following: I had some 15 soldiers from the engineers company, five or six soldiers from the staff command, and about 15 to 20 soldiers from the logistics battalion. And there were some donators too, 20 of them. And that was roughly it. Plus a remaining platoon from the 5th Battalion, an intervention platoon. So that was the mixed unit. I didn't have a complete standard type establishment unit but had to make up the unit from the men who were free from the different units, and made up a squad and a platoon for the purposes of providing an ambush. So there were about 15 soldiers from the engineers company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you use Dragan Jevtic, the commander of the engineering company, in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that the commander of that platoon, or the engineering company, should be its commander, Mr. Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so by the evening of 13 July, where were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 13th, I was at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you hear anything about Muslim prisoners on the evening of the 13th? Excuse me. At any time on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information about Muslim prisoners reached me in the evening of the 13th. I can't tell you at what time exactly. Probably between 1900 hours and 2000 hours, at least after 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you when you received that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my office, the office of the Chief of Staff, at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what form did you receive information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a telephone -- if I understood your question, it was a telephone conversation from the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade. Lieutenant Drago Nikolic called me up, and it was through him that I learnt about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did Drago Nikolic tell you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had just been called up by Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, that he had just finished talking to Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, and that he had told him that in the Zvornik area, they were expecting a large number of prisoners to be brought in from Srebrenica, or rather, from Bratunac, and that he had to make preparations to take in those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What else did he tell you? Or did you respond to him after he said that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had to be replaced as duty officer of the forward command post to be able to take part in that, and he said he was expecting a man to come with concrete, specific information as to what was to be done in this regard in future. I said -- I told him -- or first of all, I asked him why the prisoners were being taken to Zvornik, why weren't they being taken to Batkovici, down there, and then towards the north and Bijeljina, where a camp existed and where the prisoners could be put up? And he told me that the prisoners were not going to be sent towards Batkovici or the Batkovic camp, because the Batkovic camp, as everybody knew, the Red Cross and UNPROFOR knew about it, and the order was to take the prisoners and execute them in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you say when he told you that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we couldn't accept an obligation of that kind without the knowledge of our commander, and that without reporting back to the Superior Command and informing them, we couldn't do that. And he said that the order had come personally from Mladic and that everybody knew about this including our commander, Lieutenant Pandurevic. And that this would personally be implemented by Beara and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, and that they asked that he be included in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then what did you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make any comments. He told me that -- he asked where the military police company was, and asked that it be placed at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you say to that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had already deployed the military police company, that they were on assignment setting up an ambush, and that it was already deployed. And he asked that at least the commander of the military police company be placed at his disposal. Whether he was colonel or lieutenant colonel Jasikovac Miomir and have a military police platoon at least. I said I'd see what I could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, going back to where we left off at the break: You had said that: I said I'd see what I could do. At that moment in the conversation with Drago Nikolic, had you decided whether or not to support this operation to kill the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you communicated that to Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell him decisively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think you had communicated at that point to Drago Nikolic regarding whether or not you were supporting it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't think I follow you. What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your statements to him that you've told us, what were you intending to communicate to him, if anything, regarding your intentions related to the operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the military police platoon had already been engaged in the field at that point in time, while we were talking, while I was talking to him, I didn't know what was available of what he was asking me for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I knew that I couldn't place the military police platoon at his disposal. He asked for a platoon, and so it remained open. I said I would do my best to ensure something for him and to place something at his disposal, Jasikovac and some men from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say he asked you. Did he have any authority to tell you and actually take these units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked that of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but militarily, did he have the authority to take those units without asking you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you decisively ever tell him or engage him in this project?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I told him what at some point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever issue instructions or order him in any way to take part in this operation to kill the Muslim prisoners that he had told you about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously, I had practically approved -- tacitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that, what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By telling him that I would place part of the military police at his disposal. Previously, I had told him that when it becomes topical, to replace him from the forward command post for him to call up the next man to take his place, the next man in order, to all intents and purposes, I practically approved his participation in those affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your discussion about having him replaced at the forward command post take place during this first conversation you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself and Drago Nikolic, you mean? Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What else do you remember about that conversation? Anything else that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps to clarify what I mean with respect to his shift. Straight away, almost at the beginning, he told me that he would have to be replaced from the duty of duty officer at the forward command post, and I told him to see who the next man was on the list. When the time came for him to have -- to supply additional information about all this and hand over to him, to call the next man on the duty shift list, and I approved him being replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this discussion and approval of him being replaced, did that occur before or after the discussion about the killing of the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened then, after this conversation? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soon afterwards, via the radio centre, they informed me that this particular military police platoon in the ambush, observing the bridges at the Drinjaca River, noticed a vast column, a large column, and they told me that as far as they could see, it was a column three kilometres long. And with that platoon was Lieutenant Colonel Jasikovac. So when I received information from them that it was a military column with flank security, et cetera, I ordered Jasikovac to return to Zvornik with the unit. And some 40 minutes later, roughly, he did arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you order Jasikovac to return with the unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, for two reasons. The first is to place Jasikovac at the disposal of Drago Nikolic, and the second reason was the fact that the unit who was there at the ambush and remained there on the side, I had to transfer part of the unit once again in front of the column of the 28th Division. So these were the two guiding reasons I ordered them to come to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just remind us who Jasikovac was in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I wasn't precise enough. It was Miomir Jasikovac who was lieutenant of the police, military police, the military police of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Jasikovac and his unit actually show up at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers stayed in front of the barracks in the truck, and he came into my office alone. As I said a moment ago, perhaps some 40 minutes after our conversation via the radio centre and the radio device.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time was this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the evening of the 13th, in the evening, probably around 2100 hours, thereabouts, just before it became dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what occurred during the meeting you had with Mr. Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all happened in my office of the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. He informed me what they had seen, and his assessment of the column that had been sighted, and on that basis I concluded that they were large forces of the 28th Division. And then I ordered him to take five soldiers with him and for them to stay. I said that the prisoners would be brought in from the Zvornik area and that he should report to Lieutenant Colonel Drago Nikolic or that he would call him so that he should stay with those five soldiers in the Standard barracks and that the rest of the platoon that the commandeer, Commander Mekic was in charge of the remaining soldiers in the platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you tell him what was supposed to happen to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not talk about that. I just said that when he speaks to Drago Nikolic, he will see that he will give him additional orders and instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When Drago Nikolic told you that this operation was approved by Mladic and that your commander and others knew about it, why didn't you check that? Why didn't you call your commander or call someone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know if the interpretation I got was correct. You said that Mladic approved this order, and I think that I said that Drago conveyed to me that Mladic had ordered that, not approved it; ordered it. And I believed Drago Nikolic, since he told me that Mladic had ordered that to be carried out. He mentioned to me that people who would be involved in this, that the commander knew about it, quite simply, I believed him. I thought that these were matters that were far too serious for him to play games with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What should you have done when you were informed by Drago Nikolic of this operation, according to your training in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have forbidden him to do any such thing. I should have looked for Pandurevic and the Corps Commander and I should have opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you think would happen to you if you did that, if you opposed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was afraid, quite simply. After this entire chain was referred to. And at that moment, I came to the conclusion that something like that could not have happened otherwise. These people probably ordered that. And we were being kept abreast. I simply thought it was pointless for me to complain about anything then. But I should have. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many Muslim prisoners did you think Drago Nikolic was talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the afternoon of the 13th, I had already had information that this concerned about 3.000 prisoners. That is what the Zvornik Brigade was informed about, and that is what I thought it was. I did not have any more up-to-date information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After your meeting with Mr. Jasikovac, did you -- when was the next time you learned anything about the operation that you had just authorised, to kill the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information that followed in this respect, in respect of everything that was going on, was the following day, that is to say, the 14th, around 1400 hours, or roughly around that time. From Major Zoran Jovanovic, who had brought a company from Zvornik by way of reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you hear, and where were you, and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was with those units in the ambush, in the broad area of Snagovo, and he had brought in an additional company by way of reinforcement because by then we had already fought the column of the 28th Division once. He informed me that Beara brought to the area of Zvornik a large number of buses with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you say anything or do anything after receiving that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In order to just get the next few days into context, especially as it may relate to this operation to kill prisoners, could you, in the next maybe five minutes - and I know that's not a long time, but can you tell us where you went and what you did relating to your military duties from the 13th, 14th, the 15th, and 16th. And you can use the pointer and the map which is -- we have a new map, Exhibit 116. But just if you can get through those days and just try to do it in five minutes, just so that we can see the broad context of what happens within this time frame. So you could start, if you could, by telling us where you went after the meeting on the 13th, in the evening, with Jasikovac, and what you did. And I may interrupt and ask questions, as is the practice.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, on the 13th, in the evening, after having learned about this large column that had just entered the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, near the village of Glodi, immediately after that, via radio communications, using the communications that were available then, I called General Zivanovic and I informed him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remember, your words have to be translated, and I can hear the translator going pretty quick. So if you can slow it up a little bit. And before we get into this, and remember, we just want a broad, a broad outline: Could you take a look at this exhibit, P116. Do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know this map. I saw it at the time when it was made. It was made after all of the things that happened in Srebrenica happened. We can see the long time period during which it was kept. Major Galic and Major Dragutinovic signed it. We can see it here. The assistant commander of staff for operations and teaching, he was not that during the Srebrenica events. He was assistant commander for personnel at the time. At that time, at the Srebrenica time, Major Dragutinovic was assistant commander for operations. However, this map here, or rather, this part around the Zvornik Brigade, this was done as far back as 1993. So the first signature comes from that period, lest there be any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And remember, we have to make a record. So when you point -- you pointed down to those two names that were involved with this map. They are the names in Cyrillic down in the right corner of the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the various coloured markings on this map, just the big ones, what they represent, and what this map represents, just briefly, if you could. If you can start down in the southern part of the map and work your way north.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this is a topographical map. 1 to 50.000. In the centre of the map is the municipality of Zvornik, or rather, the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. There are some handwritten decisions - sorry - markings on the map, according to the rules of keeping topographical maps in the JNA and the VRS. Then also there are general names and the names of particular units that are printed in black. So, for example, there is the name of the map itself, in black. The markings of the units, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, the Drina Corps, then the legend, and so on. All of that is written in black. As for the red colour, it denotes our units, the VRS units, and their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the blue markings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the blue markings on the map represent our then enemy, that is to say, the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And here we see these markings operative group 4. This does not match the actual situation in the month of July 1995. I've already said that, as it can be seen here, this map was kept from 1993 onwards, and that is when they had this kind of organisation. They had divisions by 1995, and brigades. But these markings are there because it's an old map. So all the blue markings on the map relate to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, units and their actual movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the title says, up top.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is marked as the "working map of the operative organ of the command of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade." It was -- the beginning is the 1st of September, 1993, meaning that it was kept from the 1st of September, 1993, and the end is 31st of December, 1995. According to the rules then in force all such documents were strictly confidential. So that is the copy of the document that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I apologise. I understand it's in Cyrillic. But can you tell us what this marking is, the two-letter marking ending in "X," right below the title.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The X is H in Cyrillic, and it says RH here, which is an abbreviation for the Republic of Croatia, Republika Hrvatska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you go down to the next three-letter abbreviation, below that. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm showing right now? IBK, IBK. That is the Eastern Bosnia Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go across the Drina, and it looks like a C.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an S in Cyrillic. SRJ in Cyrillic, which is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Savezna Republika Jugoslavija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go down to the two-letter area that you're pointing to in the southern part of the map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: DK, the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then down in the south, where we have the red and the blue again in the right-hand corner of the map, what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you mean this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. The red markings and the blue markings, the circle.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in the south of this map, is the area of the enclave of Srebrenica. The blue colour, as I said a few minutes ago, depicts positions within the enclave that were held by the units of the 28th Division. The colour red depicts the positions of units of the Army of Republika Srpska that were facing the positions of the 28th Division, that is to say, those that were manning the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there's little red arrows in that enclave area. What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These arrows show the directions of advancement and penetration of the Army of Republika Srpska units during the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go to the north of the enclave. There appears to be a semicircle in the north of the enclave with -- in blue, with arrows going in a northerly direction. What is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This semi-circle at the north of the enclave is marked in blue. This is a topographical marking for denoting a unit that is expected, units that are being collected. If I remember correctly, this is the villages of Jaglici and Susnjari, that area where the 28th Division was being grouped, and all the accompanying manpower, for starting the breakthrough and the march towards the area of the 2nd Corps. And this -- so this is the region of build-up. And the arrows going from there show the direction of their movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you point out the village -- I know the Court can't possibly see that from there, but can you point out where the village of Potocari is, just so the Court can get an idea of where it fits into this. If you yourself -- just generally. I know you can't even read it from there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I approach the map and read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That gets problematic, just logistically. If you need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, can we have the camera zoom on certain points? Maybe the witness could read from the monitor.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really cannot see a thing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I can't either. My machine is not working. But it's a good idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So now you're pointing to the area of Potocari. Were you able to lean over and spot it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't see from here, but roughly it should be somewhere around here, the village of Potocari, around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's all we need, is roughly. And how about Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you follow the road to Konjevic Polje, just slowly with your red ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now you're stopped at Konjevic Polje. Okay. And can you take --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- The main road are up to Zvornik from Konjevic Polje, with your red dot.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's Zvornik, where you stopped. Where is the forward command post that Drago Nikolic was talking to you from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that's in the area of what battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And all those battalions are marked by number on this map?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the north is the 1st, and then the next one is the 5th, then the 2nd, and the 3rd, then the 6th, then the 4th, and then the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you point out the rough northern boundary of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The northern boundary of the Drina Corps coincides with the northern boundary of the area of the Zvornik infantry Brigade. I've already mentioned that today during the course of the day. This is a geographical notion. Konjski Put, Tursan Brdo is the name of the actual village at the front line itself. And then 141 was the trig in the village of Glavicice on the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've pointed to that on the map also. Is there a little red line between those two points that you can make out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the road is marked on the map, but this roughly coincides with the uppermost northern boundary of the Zvornik Brigade and the Drina Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you point out roughly where Pilica is. I don't think you're going to be able to see it but do you know roughly where Pilica is, below the border of the Zvornik Brigade, Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably here, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's just about an inch below the area that you've described as the -- sorry. Let's say two centimetres below the area you described as the border. All right. Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted the record to reflect that the Defence is allowing the Prosecution to lead this witness through this combat offensive so that it's clear for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. This is just some positions, local positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's no problem on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you back to where we had started before, but remember, we need to do -- try to do this in five minutes, if you can. Just describe to us the military situation from the evening on the 13th when you go out to the lines to, let's say, the morning of the 17th, just so we can get a feel for the situation. And again, if you need to refer to the map, just let us know what location so we can try to make the record clear. If you could tell us where you go on the evening of the 13th. Let's do it in five minutes, if we can. I think that should make a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. McCloskey, I've already said that during the 12th and the 13th, the command of the Zvornik Brigade and the command of the Drina Corps, to my mind, had a very confused picture as to what was going on in relation to the column of the 28th Division. Very many pieces of misinformation, perhaps I can put it that way. However, by the evening I realised that there was a large column in the village of Glodi, and they entered the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and that finally some concrete action has to be taken in that respect. At Snagovo, I already had part of the units from the night of the 12th and from the afternoon of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Can you show us roughly where the border is that you're talking about between the Zvornik Brigade and your neighbour and where you first became aware that the Muslim units entered. It can just be rough. Don't worry about being precise at this point.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already shown the northern border a while ago when we talked about the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and this is the boundary on the south and our neighbour was the 1st Bircani Brigade and Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're going fast. Especially now we've got to keep it slow.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Our neighbour on the left was the infantry brigade from Sekovici, the Bircanska Brigade, and the left zone went along the Spreca River, the Spreca River, and then went on to Mount Udrc. Then to the confluence of Drinjaca and Zeleni Jadar, those two rivers, then there is Milovan, and then above the village of Zelinja to the Drina River. Already in this area, Kuslat and Milovan, that is where the Bratunac Brigade was our neighbour, in that area. So that would be within these boundaries. That was the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Now, where we first saw the column clearly entering the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade was when they were crossing the Drina River - sorry, the Drinjaca River. And when they were entering the area of the village of Glodi. It's somewhere around here. I cannot see very well from the spot I'm sitting at, but it's around here. This is where we first saw them. Our patrols and our platoons that were in the ambush saw them there around dusk. I've already said that part of the units from earlier on, from the night of the 12th, were there, and then they were reinforced on the afternoon of the 13th, with Maric's company, and the engineers we mentioned. Not only the engineers. I mentioned other units in that context as well. They were sent to Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I notice on the map there seems to be blue arrows going across red lines. What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depicts graphically the actual combat and the development of the situation. Because on the morning of the 14th, we had the first combat with part of the column of the 28th Division. And afterwards, in the early evening hours of the 14th, we had fiercer fighting, and the units that I was with were broken up there, left and right.
