And then they penetrated this asphalt road, Crni Vrh, and then they went here to the village of Planinci and towards Krizevici and Baljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what dates and times did they make it to the Baljkovica area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front of the column of the 28th Division in the village of Baljkovica, which was within the area of our 4th infantry Battalion. They got there in the early evening hours of the 15th, perhaps roughly around 1700 hours or 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again, describe in broad terms what happened after the evening hours of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 15th, these units which were organised in such a way as to defend the area from the onslaught of the 28th Division were surrounded in that valley of Baljkovica, and that's when the fighting started in the encirclement. The column of the 28th Division broke through to this area and was just two to three kilometres away from the 2nd Corps of the BH army, and that's where the severe fighting began. There would be a lull and then the fighting would start up again. But the fighting and battles were continuous, to all intents and purposes, throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say they broke through this area, what do you mean? Can you give us a village or an area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the 28th Division broke through into the broad area around the village of Baljkovica, and parts of them came to Krizevici, Motovo, Potocani, those villages. I think there was the village of Rebici as well, that that's what the village was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what time was this fierce fighting? What day and what time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The serious fighting started already on the evening of the 15th. Then, during the night, there was a thunderstorm, a lot of rain, and during the night our units which were stationed there lost their positions at Grujic Groblje. In the early morning hours of the 16th, the mortar company was practically destroyed, and three self-propelled vehicles were taken over on these positions at Motovska Kosa and the culmination of the fighting came in the morning hours, probably around 0400 hours, 4.00 a.m., as dawn was breaking on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During this combat with the 28th Division coming up from the south, were the 2nd Corps positions that are marked on the map in blue, were they engaged in this fight at all from the north and the west?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely correct. The 2nd Corps already in this area of responsibility of the Birac Brigade, our left neighbour, started offensive combat operations on the 11th of July. On the 12th, our 7th Battalion came under attack, and in that same period, it was in the area of the 6th Battalion that some demonstrative operations were taking place. But as the column of the 28th Division drew closer to the front part of the 2nd Corps, the units of the 2nd Corps itself and their divisions in that area, strengthened their pressure, exerted greater pressure, and after the night, and on the 14th, in this area here, roughly this area, it is a mountain wreath, in actual fact - the units of the 2nd Corps of the BH army made large bonfires, and these fires could be seen from this broad area here. That was probably a marker of some kind of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... So we could go back to it for the record if need be.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it from here, but if I remember correctly, the hill was called Barasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On this map, it's right below the three initials. Can you tell us what those three initials are again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the OG-4 initial, which means Operative Group 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So then just continue your -- these bonfires were lit by the Muslims, and you left off: There was heavy fighting on the 16th and the early morning hours. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was heavy fighting, and this continued for the whole of the morning of the 16th. The Baljkovica area was constantly under artillery fire, either from our side or from the Muslim side. But everything was aflame in that area, and this group of units within the command post of the 4th Battalion, which is where I was myself, found itself surrounded and cut off from the rest of the units, and this happened on the 15th -- on the evening of the 15th. They weren't able to evacuate their wounded. So it was a chaotic situation. And at one point on the 16th, probably around 10.00 - anyway, in the early morning hours of the 16th - the unit of the 2nd Corps -- the units of the 2nd Corps here in the region of the river of Baljkovica, underneath the village of Nezuk, managed to gain control of the positions of the 4th Battalion and to break through this front flank, the Grjesnik, as we called it. But this was in a very narrow portion of the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the 16th, I was ordered at one point - I think it was around noon - or rather, something was approved, that I could start my own evacuation and the evacuation of those units, the withdrawal from the command of 4th Battalion towards the positions of the 6th Battalion, towards Parlog. That was approved. And we managed to break through until the halfway point, a village called Glovedarice and on the basis of radio communication I received orders from the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, to cease the fighting and to undertake negotiations with Semso Muminovic, who was an officer from the command of one of those divisions from the 2nd Corps of the BH army. In order to establish a truce and to open a corridor for the passage of the 28th Division, which was already there in the area. They had already taken up the command post and set fire to it where I was in Paljkovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that in fact happen? Was there a corridor opened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a little later on, after a series of problems of a practical nature, practical obstacles, the corridor was opened towards the village of Nezuk, that access and direction, and the commander, Lieutenant Pandurevic, issued orders that in addition to this position that had been seized of our squad that we deal with another platoon of the 4th Battalion and that along that axis, along a small river and in a valley, to open -- that was where the corridor was opened for the passage of the column of the 28th Division. And we actually agreed on a provisional truce, ceasefire. I think that was on the 16th, at 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did that corridor remain open for the departure of the Muslim column?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had agreed on this corridor, and the first variant of the agreement was that the corridor should be open for 24 hours, that it should remain open for 24 hours. If it was opened on the 16th at 1400 hours, then until the 17th at 1400 hours. However, the next day -- or rather, while this was going on, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic and someone else, Semso Muminovic - I don't know what he was by rank, probably a colonel or something like that - they had radio communication. They were communicating by radio. And in the morning of the 17th, Semso asked that the corridor be left open for a further 24 hours. However, our commander did not approve that, and extended the deadline for another two hours. So from 1400 hours until 1600 hours. However, our units started moving at around 1500 hours to start the corridor. I think the corridor was actually closed at 1600 hours at the latest. But the units starting closing it off a little while before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many Muslims were able to make it through the corridor while it was open?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is, to give you an estimate, on the basis of what we were able to see. Through that section, the column started moving from 1400 hours. There was only some sporadic fire, but neither side fired, actually. And after the column -- after 1400 hours, the column was still passing through, until it got dark. So I think a large number managed to pass through. I was negotiating in Baljkovica, at the headquarters there, on the 16th, in the morning, with an officer from the command of the 28th Division. He introduced himself as being captain Salihovic, and told me that he was an officer, an operative officer in the command of the 28th Division. He had been wounded and as he wasn't able to talk because he had a neck injury, he wrote down on a piece of paper that they had 7.000 people in the vicinity, of which 3.000 were armed. That's what he told me then and that's all I know. And that would be my best guess and answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you thought the information he was giving you was credible, based on everything else you knew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought he was telling the truth and that there were probably about 7.000 of them. And on a previous occasion, I had the opportunity of talking -- on the 15th, in the morning, with two Muslim soldiers who had been captured from the same column, and they told me on that occasion that the column of the 28th Division had split into three parts and that each part had approximately 2.000 men marching one behind the other. So that would make it 6.000. That's what they told me then, and this would roughly coincide with what the captain told me subsequently, a day later, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: During this fierce fighting on the 15th and 16th, how many of the VRS soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me, about 40, 38, 39 soldiers were killed, and over 100 wounded. It was very fierce fighting at close range. We were about 50 metres apart. So it was almost breast to breast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you known any fighting like that ever occurring in that war before this time, with those kinds of casualties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in quite a number of battles throughout the war, and this was one of the fiercest fighting that I had taken part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslims were killed in this fighting on the 15th and 16th, have any idea?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific, but they must have had considerable losses, a lot of people killed, and even more wounded, because we used all the weapons at our disposal, the technical equipment, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did the Muslims do with their dead?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume they pulled them out during the night, between the 16th and 17th. That's just my assumption. We did not find a large number of corpses in the area later on. I don't remember exactly how many, but maybe about 20. That was all. In this area around Baljkovica, on the 17th -- on the evening of the 17th up to the 19th, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As far as you know, did the VRS make any effort to bury those corpses of Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. Perhaps it might have been on the 19th that we buried the bodies at Motovska Kosa, somewhere up there. We might have buried these 15 to 20 bodies that we had gathered together. Our units arrived, so we had to collect up the bodies, and they were buried there in that general area of Motovska Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of the engineering unit or any unit of the Zvornik military or civilian authorities burying any battle casualties prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean burying the dead who were killed in battle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was quite confused by the question too, because so far we have no evidence that the engineering department has buried anyone, and now he's asking the question: Before this time, has the engineer company participated in asanacija before. So could he please just break the question down and clear up his questioning in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. The question is not clear to us too. Would you please rephrase it, lay some foundations on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of, prior to the burial of the battle casualties that you just described on the 19th or 20th, were you aware of the engineering unit of the Zvornik Brigade burying any other battle casualties for the fighting that occurred between the 15th and the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I haven't heard any testimony that the engineering department participated in this burial, so could he lay the proper foundation and predicate first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Keep your first question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You put two questions in one. This is a compound question. Just stick to your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any burials of Muslim battle casualties from the fighting on the 15th and 16th, aside from what you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you asked about the burials of the killed Muslim soldiers during the fighting, during the battle that I described. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter did not catch your answer. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try to clear it up, Your Honour. It's a difficult area, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've described the burial of casualties on the 19th or 20th of July. Are you aware of any other battle casualty burials that occurred before that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Killed Muslim soldiers in battle during the breakthrough of the column of the 28th Division, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you very briefly describe the situation in the area around Baljkovica and the general area of the Zvornik Brigade relating to remaining Muslim groups after the 17th of July. Just roughly, what went on, just to give us an idea.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already stated, the bulk of the column of the 28th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honour, to interfere here, but I think that we're missing a very important piece of information. I don't think Mr. McCloskey has ever asked who participated in the burial of the Muslim soldiers, and I think I'm waiting to see where his connection is of the burial with the Muslim soldiers and where it's relevant to the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to me, it's very clear. But if you want to stress on this point, we may ask Mr. McCloskey to ask the question to the witness so that this issue could be settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The burials of battle casualties, that was done by the Zvornik Brigade, as you stated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what unit or body did that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Collecting the bodies in the area around Baljkovica was conducted by the units who happened to be there, deployed there, in combat formation. Now, the actual digging, burial, was done by machines from the engineering company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, the Geneva Conventions, there's no problem with burying battle casualties, is there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could just get to the broad outlines of the situation after the corridor is closed. Can you describe the next days and next regarding the number of Muslims in the area and what the Zvornik Brigade was doing about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the next few days, after the corridor had been closed, on the afternoon of the 17th, the units of the 2nd Corps launched several attacks, probably with the aim of breaking down the brigade's defence in the area, and they attacked most frequently on the 7th, 6th, and 4th Battalion, which had already suffered considerable losses, casualties. Now, the area that the column of the 28th Division moved around from Baljkovica southwards to the end of our area, the village of Glodi, was in fact -- I don't know whether I'm going to use the right term and expression, but there were probably a lot of stragglers or remaining groups. Whether they had remained consciously or whether they had just gone astray and lost their way or anything like that while the column was passing through. So that the units from the Zvornik Brigade, with reinforcements which had arrived on the evening of the 16th or the morning of the 17th or during the day of the 17th, took over the search operation. They searched the terrain, destroyed and captured these groups, and I think that I should stress in this regard that in all these activities of searching the terrain, units of the MUP joined in. So searching the terrain and dealing with the stragglers and remaining groups of the column of the 28th Division, this was done intensively towards almost the end of the months, that is to say, the 30th of July. Afterwards, there would be searches from time to time, occasional ambushes. But after July, the intensity lessened of our involvement with respect to controlling the area in depth and searching the terrain, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us any kind of a rough estimate of how many Muslim stragglers, as you've called them, were in the area of the Zvornik Brigade during this time period, from when the corridor closed to the end of July, and onward?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our assessment that we were dealing with a large number, fairly large number. According to the information that reached us, they had split into smaller groups, numbering five to ten men. Very rarely were there groups of about a hundred. Once or twice in an area, but mostly these large groups were readily visible, so they broke up into smaller groups. And towards the end of the month, as I've already said, all these groups moved in the traces of the 28th Division, in their steps, towards Baljkovica. After that time, they no longer moved towards Baljkovica, but redirected and went to the Udrc area and towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Right after the corridor closed, was there any policy from the Zvornik Brigade command relating to capturing prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th, after the -- after one of our soldiers was killed and several other wounded, the commander ordered that nothing should be risked when prisoners were captured, that our units should not expose themselves to further risk, should not run any more risk. So after that, some units did not take prisoners. What they did was to kill them on the spot. However, others did continue the process of capturing the prisoners if they came across anybody. But generally, a few days later, the commander -- I think it was on the 20th or the 21st - did away with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say "killed them on the spot," are you talking about in a combat situation or are you talking improperly, after they have been captured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go back, if we can - thank you for that overview - and let's go back to the 14th of July, where you have described your last contact about information related to the operation to kill Muslims. You'd heard about that Beara was coming with many Muslims. Again, I'm sorry. Can you just tell us about what time you got that information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, since you are changing the subject, could we have our break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would love a break. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, as we were going back to the 14th, could you just briefly remind us of the contact you -- information you got from Beara. What time was that? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was at Snagovo, roughly where the intersection of the roads is up there. There were -- it was probably about 1400 hours that afternoon. Major Zoran Jovanovic brought a company by way of reinforcement, and he informed me, as I already said, that Colonel Beara had brought to Zvornik a large number of prisoners, or rather, that buses with prisoners of war that Beara had brought arrived in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do anything about that information, act on it in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you think that information had to do with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the arrival of these prisoners was related to the information from the previous evening when I talked to Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. That's what he had conveyed to me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When is the next time on the 14th that you had any information about the operation to kill the Muslim prisoners, I mean related to the Muslim prisoners coming to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that same day, somewhat later, my signalman received a message over the radio which was not extended to him but to the signalman of Captain Maric, and the radio centre was conveying a message from the operations centre that two engineers should go back to Zvornik. Those who were up there with us in the ambush. Specific names were referred to, and allegedly they were supposed to go there to build a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do when you got that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became suspicious. I thought it probably could not involve any kind of road. My initial idea was that perhaps somebody is trying to get those two persons out of combat, or that it has to do something with another job. So I called the radio centre and I asked them to check this out, what it was all about specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have any suspicions what that "another job" might be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that perhaps they could be used for burials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Burials of what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the executed prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I asked, through the radio centre, to have this checked out, to see what this was about. And for a short period of time -- within a short period of time, after five or six minutes perhaps, I got the following information: That they were being requested to come to Zvornik because of the job that was being carried out by Beara, Popovic, and Nikolic, and I knew what that was, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you just for the record tell us what you thought Beara, Popovic, and Nikolic's job was at that point, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Execution of the said prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do once you received that information about those individuals being involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I was touring the units that were there within the ambush, and I went on until I came to that platoon of Dragan Jevtic that was a bit further away, about 100 metres away. Jevtic had already received that message, and I think that he was already in a discussion with these men, these two men specifically, these machine experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of those two men, machine experts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One was Mitrovic, nicknamed Kocanj, and the other one, I can't remember his name right now. At any rate, their names were referred to specifically through radio communications. They were not being requested by way of the duties they had but by name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what did you do when you went over to where Dragan Jevtic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he saw that I was coming, Dragan Jevtic spoke to me and conveyed to me what I had already known, that they were asking for these two mentioned men to be sent to Zvornik. I said that he should release them and not discuss it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did he feel about releasing those men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think, or rather, the impression I had was that he was against that. He probably thought that he needed them there for combat. There weren't enough of them, anyway. My impression was that he would not have let them go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he follow your order to let them go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just go back briefly. You mentioned your radio signalman got this message originally. Can you describe for us what kind of radio equipment you had with you while you were in the field there and what kind of personnel you had to help operate that equipment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, this group that was up there with me at Snagovo, in an ambush, we used standard radio stations, RUP-12 radios, that did not have any protection possibilities. We knew that the other side could be listening in. The signalmen who operated the equipment were soldiers, the men who carried this equipment too. They were in charge of this radio communication. And in a way - how shall I put this - in order to prevent us from being overheard, at least up to a point, there were about 15 or 20 other frequencies that were written out and then sometimes as we were speaking we would move to those frequencies, with the intention of being overheard as little as possible. I should probably point out in this context that these signalmen who carried this radio equipment were not very well trained, and it wasn't easy for them to handle all of this. So probably the enemy side could hear quite a bit, especially if there was fighting that was about to break out and if there were to be a combat situation or something, then all of this could be listened into even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the preparation of your case, did you have an opportunity to look at some of the intercepts provided by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Your office, through my lawyers, submitted that to me. I saw these intercepts that the enemy side that was listening in to what we were saying recorded. I looked through all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your review of that, the material, did you find anything that appeared to be relevant to this conversation -- or the information you received about the named engineering people that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the page where the intercepts for the 14th are, I came across this message conveyed to Captain Maric, and specifically, two names are recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. McCloskey is going into the whole topic of military intercepts by the Bosnian and Herzegovina army at this time, the BiH army. Of course, the one he's referring to, we have double objections to, because Mr. Obrenovic is not a participant, he's speculating, he was not present at the time that these communications were given or received. But as far as the total group of intercepts that he's trying to introduce, there's only one, I believe, that Mr. Obrenovic is a participant in. Our only objection there would be lack of authenticity, lack of reliability, because of the equipment used by the Muslim tactical field operators at the place where they were receiving, and we intend to challenge the authenticity and reliability of all of the intercepts. But the one he's about to go into, Mr. Obrenovic is not a participant in the conversation, and he can't -- I mean, he can identify the names of the operators, but he can do that without saying that it was related to or corroborated by an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I think we have these question settled during the previous occasion. Of course, on the one hand, you have the full right to challenge the authenticity of those intercepts. There's no problem about it. And one of the criteria to admit them into the evidence is that those sources should be reliable. There's no problem about that. But here we have this witness with us. It doesn't matter that the Prosecution asks some questions about these intercepts. Although this witness was not a participant or mentioned in the intercepts, but he could shed some light about the people involved in those intercepts. We are here -- we are not discussing about admission of the evidence into these intercepts, but we have to be helped by some background information about those intercepts, especially the contents. We could not -- well, I think it's possible, but it's not convenient for us to call this witness whenever we need him. Since this witness is here, we'll go through those intercepts, and later on we'll consider his testimony with some other witnesses. And at last, if the reliability of these intercepts, authenticity of these intercepts, are established, we'll consider whether to admit those into the evidence. But this is at a very late stage. I'm looking forward, Ms. Sinatra, to your cooperation in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will, of course, put on that evidence in cross-examination. I would just like for the record that we object to any testimony relating to the intercepts at this time, for lack of proper foundation and reliability. And we will -- I know the Court will rule on that when we go to offer the exhibits into evidence at that time. I would like to also object that since he doesn't have personal knowledge of this, that it violates the Rules of Evidence of personal knowledge. He should be speaking from his own personal knowledge of these matters. And that's my objection. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that your objection is well recorded in the transcript. We'll bear in mind your objections. As for whether this person has the personal knowledge or not, we don't know at this moment. We have to hear what this witness is going to tell us. Maybe the question is not about the specific issue mentioned in the intercepts. It may be related to certain persons in that particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And Your Honour, we agree. If he has personal knowledge about those people, that he can relate in the courtroom, separate from the intercepts, then we would most certainly have no objections to that. I also would like to ask the Court ahead of time: Mr. McCloskey has been asking the witness, not today in Court, but he asked whether he thinks this intercept is genuine. I think that's an improper question to ask from someone who has no experience in the communications field and didn't participate in the conversation. So we would just like to have a running objection that genuine is not a proper terminology for verification of an intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course, we'll consider those testimonies, taking into consideration of your objections and with the understanding that this witness could give us some evidence. But as for how much weight we are going to put on that evidence is another matter. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you inform us how close you are to your signalman when you're in the field in a combat situation, and the information he provides you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Usually a step away. Only if there would be shooting, then we would move from one place to another. He would be right next to my shoulder or I would be right next to his shoulder. It's all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so when your signalman informed you of this information regarding these two engineers, can you tell us how close he was to you and how -- if you know, how -- well, can you tell us how close he was to you when he told you about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said: A step away. Let's say a metre away. We were right next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know when he had received the information over the radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you know how long before he told -- passed on that information to you he had received it on the radio?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately. Very soon afterwards, perhaps a few seconds later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you happen to overhear any of that information over the radio as it came to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a headphone on his ears, and I heard that something was being said, but he was the one who was conveying it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back to the question: When you were looking at the Prosecution intercepts, did you find any intercept that appeared related to this information you've just talked about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I found precisely that message, where it said Maric, or for Captain Maric - I can't remember exactly - and then the specific name and surname is mentioned, Mitrovic, and I don't know what the first name is, and the other one, that they should come to Nedjo's restaurant in order to build a road. I think that that's exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. President, at the conclusion I will have some exhibits. That will be one of the exhibits. But I think it will go more smoothly if we just save those exhibits at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Whatever way you think is suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So about what time were these two engineers actually released from their combat duties on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Jevtic and I spoke to each other, they left, perhaps a few minutes after that. So all of that happened after 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how long after 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So after that, on the 14th, did you receive any other information relating to the operation to kill the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th, late in the afternoon, in a conversation that took place through radio communications with the commander of the 4th Battalion - this was just before our attack against the village of Liplje - I found out that there were some problems in Orahovac and that the deputy commander of the 4th Battalion had sent a group of soldiers to help out there. All of this was via radio communications, and we did not speak openly. We tried to improvise, in order to prevent the other side from recording what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So can you describe -- now, I'm sorry. Did you take part in this improvised conversation yourself or was it with your signalman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on our radio, and from the 4th Battalion, it was their signalman who was on line. So I took the headphone, the receiver, from the signalman, and I did the talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe this improvised conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was getting ready for us to launch the attack against Liplje, I wanted to see what the situation was in the 4th Battalion that was remaining behind our back. I called the command, the headquarters there, and I said that -- and they said that everything was all right towards the 2nd Corps and towards the front end. But they said that there was a problem at the place where are the command of our brigade was previously, as well as the commander of that battalion. That means Orahovac. And that there were problems in relation to those who had been brought in, the Zoljani. They were the intervention platoon and they were with Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic in Srebrenica. So I knew what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were you speaking to at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarity, might I ask that the Prosecutor, who has given us a huge book of exhibits with numbers on it, if he's referring to one of the intercepts, can he tell us which one he's referring to so I can at least look at what he's speaking about at the same time? Just for identification purposes, not to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it possible? I believe that Mr. McCloskey said that he will introduce those documents at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I made specific reference, as you've stated, to the previous conversation about the engineers. But this conversation was not intercepted, the conversation that he had with the person that he's talking about now. There's no record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I guess that's what I was confused, Your Honour, because I'm looking for one, and he's not provided us with that information. I will object that if there was no recording and no intercept and no way to corroborate this testimony, that it violates the best -- the Rule of Evidence as far as reliability and authenticity goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this piece of information is different from the previous one. Because this witness, he himself took part in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think you are correct on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who were you talking to during this conversation about the -- you referred to, I think, the Zoljani.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one side was I, myself, and on the other side was one of the signalman from the command of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you communicating at this time with the deputy commander of the 4th Battalion in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his signalman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if the deputy commander was around his signalman anywhere and communicating through him, or do you think you were just speaking directly to the signalman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His signalman was right next to him, just like my signalman was right next to me. It is generally known that signalmen only convey messages. They don't reach decisions or make reports. They just convey what we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who was the deputy commander of the 4th Battalion that you were communicating with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Lieutenant Lazar Ristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you act on that information at this time at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was my understanding of this message that they had resolved the problems and that the 4th Battalion had no problems. So I could therefore proceed with my activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so in the evening of the 14th, did you have any significant communications that you made to anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, on the 14th, during the day, I had conversations with the radio centre several times. My intention was to inform them of the real strength of the column and to ask for reinforcements. On the 14th, late at night, probably after 2300 hours, when we had gathered together our dispersed units, and when I gained a general impression of the casualties and losses and what had actually happened to us, I took a piece of paper and wrote down a brief outline of what had happened to us, and titled it "Extraordinary report," and gave it to the signalman to convey to the radio centre, communications centre, and to be relayed to the duty officer and the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just remind us: You've spoken of the radio centre. Can you just describe to us briefly again the difference between the radio centre and the duty office, and their locations and functions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the radio communications centre was a container, actually, situated on a hill above Zvornik, above the barracks at Karakaj, perhaps some 500 metres from the barracks itself, in the direction of -- or rather, north-west, in a northwesterly direction, which was where there was a squad of soldiers. And with their radios, they had communication with our units in the field, and also with me and my group up there. And so it was from there that they had a line, a wire line, to the headquarters, which is where the duty officer had his office, as I explained to you yesterday. The office was on the first floor, the first room to the right after you came up the stairs. So I and the operations duty officer could not have a direct link and communication. They had to call or I had to call up the radio communications centre and they would then relay the messages to each of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us why there wasn't a radio centre inside the Zvornik Brigade headquarters that you could communicate with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think you were there. The Zvornik Brigade headquarters, or rather, the entire barracks, are located in a valley, gorge, and they wouldn't be able to have any radio communication. The radio waves would be blocked by the large -- the mountains round about. So the geography of the terrain was such that it demanded radio communication in this way rather than in the other way. So that's what we did. The tactical capabilities of the devices we had and the structure of the terrain itself, the geographic make-up, dictated how we structured our communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That evening of the 14th, did you have any other significant -- or did you have any communications that related to the operation to kill the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you stay the night of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent the night of the 14th together with those units, at Snagovo, in the area of the crossroads up there. So between us and Zvornik was where this column of the 28th Division passed through. We were cut away from the Zvornik area, actually, cut off from the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on the 14th of July, did you ever go back to the brigade headquarters at any time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware that an officer of the Zvornik Brigade military police, I believe her first name was Nada, provided a statement to the OTP said she saw you at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade on the evening of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm going to object to this line of questioning. Mr. McCloskey is questioning the witness on whether he read OTP witness statements of someone else, and whether he can speculate what it is that she was thinking or saying at the time. I think it's an improper line of questioning. If he has Nada Stojanovic's statement that he'd like to base this foundation upon, we'd be happy to accept it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the transcript, the witness gives some evidence, saying that he was not at headquarters on that night; he was at Snagovo, in the areas of the crossroads up there. Then the Prosecution tried to refresh the memory of this witness, saying that: Well, I have a different view on that, because somebody said that you were at headquarters on the 14th. I think that's a quite normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, all we're asking from the Jokic Defence, is if Mr. McCloskey is going to ask the witness if he's refreshed his memory with a document that is an OTP statement, that they introduce that document into evidence, in support of the memory that he has. It's like him refreshing his memory here with documents in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Let us hear how the witness is going to answer this question, and later on we'll decide whether we'll have this document or not. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, do you know the person I'm talking about? Do you know Nada's last name, for the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it was Mrs. Nada Stojanovic, who was a senior in the company of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you account for her version of events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. That calls for speculation on his part to comment on how does he account for Nada Stojanovic's perspective on the events. The best witness would be Nada Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree that question is not quite clear. Maybe, Mr. McCloskey, you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you agree with Nada Stojanovic's assessment that you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, she must be wrong on that point. I wasn't there. I don't know why she said that. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall reading the statement of a soldier from the Bratunac Brigade named Mico Gavric that also reported you present at the Bratunac Brigade on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm just going to renew the objection with each statement that he's referring to, that the witness refreshed his memory with, if he'd like to introduce those documents into evidence so that we can see the documents that he refreshed his memory with, we would not object to any introduction of those statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't know how important, whether this witness in the headquarters or in other places. Secondly, maybe the Prosecution at first would like to refresh the memory of this witness to see what is his response. If the Prosecution failed, the Prosecution might show a document to this witness. We'll just wait. We'll just be patient for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to clarify: It is not my intention to refresh the recollection of this witness. He has, I believe, full recollection of the events. But I do know from the record that these two soldiers differ in their account with this witness, and it will be a very -- an area that I'm sure counsel will like to bring up on cross-examination. And as such, I wanted to give this witness a chance to explain any knowledge he has of those differences, which is my duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we have no objection, if Mr. Obrenovic had personal knowledge from a conversation with Mico Gavric or Nada Stojanovic about their not agreeing with his version of the story. But the fact that the Prosecutor used his statements that he does not intend to introduce into evidence to refresh the witness's memory is inappropriate and we object to it, unless he wants to introduce those statements into evidence as a foundation for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I saw two counsels standing. And this time I think I'll call Mr. Karnavas first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could be of some assistance. I believe if the Prosecution were to ask Mr. Obrenovic if in the course of his preparation did he come across any documents presented to him by the Prosecution which would very -- or be different from his recollection, and the answer is yes, then he could probably ask the next question. And in one of those documents, and I don't think that there would be a problem. And so we certainly don't intend to object. We do recognise -- we understand we have the statements, but I think a lot of confusion can just be put to rest if he were to ask: In the preparation, did you come across any documents which are different from your recollection as to where you were. And he'll say yes of course. Which are the documents he'll say a statement from Mico Gavric and what did he say. We can have that little discourse and we can move on. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I really appreciate the instruction from Mr. Karnavas on how we should proceed, but I believe that I agree with Mr. McCloskey on this that the best evidence would be to have Nada Stojanovic or Mico Gavric come into the courtroom and testify. And the fact that he has referred to a document that the witness has refreshed his memory with, questioning is still inappropriate unless he wants to introduce the document which is the foundation of the testimony into record. But I do agree: Nada Stojanovic is on the witness list of the Prosecutor, and at that time Mr. McCloskey can question Ms. Stojanovic on, you know, her difference of opinion from Mr. Obrenovic. But the fact that Mr. Obrenovic has not spoken to Ms. Stojanovic, the fact that he's relying on everything he says right now from reading a hearsay statement from the Prosecution which he does not intend to introduce into evidence is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the issue here, at least at this moment, in my view, is not a crucial matter. It only goes to the credibility of this witness. Because this witness has already admitted the crime that is prosecution [sic], the crime against humanity. Since this is not a crucial issue, and during the proceedings there are always different views concerning with certain things happened. Here we just hear what the witness is going to tell us. If the Defence counsel would like to rebuttal the views expressed by this witness, you probably would show the document to him and argue with him to attack his credibility. And later on we will have that person to be a live witness in this courtroom. I believe that at last the Chamber will piece all the information together and to make decisions. So let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I just wanted to bring to the Court's attention that one of the main issues in the defence case is Mr. Obrenovic's presence or not presence on the day of the 14th in the Zvornik Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may raise it during your cross-examination and in your case, in the future. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, you I believe testified you spent the night of the 14th in the field. Can you briefly describe what you did the morning of the 15th and where you went.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, early on the morning of the 15th, an all-out attack started on the threefold battalion, that is the 7th, 4th, and 6th. The group who was at Snagovo with me, when dawn broke, consolidated our positions, and from Borik, from Snagovo, we moved towards Crni Vrh, searching the terrain. The idea was that at Crni Vrh, at the asphalt road, that we should joined up with units of the 7th Battalion who was there to protect their rear and was in the ambush there. So we were moving along this ridge towards Crni Vrh, searching the terrain as we went, and I personally was in command of the units up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime around 11.00 I returned to the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you go back to the HQ, headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned because the column of the 28th Division, the bulk of the column, had already crossed over the Zvornik-Crni Vrh asphalt road and went to Planinci and came out just in the rear of the 4th, 7th, and 6th Battalion. And I went to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, the headquarters, to take steps to ask for reinforcements or do anything I could to protect those three battalions of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you get back to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see when you got to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road - I took the old road with the forces from Zvornik - and on the asphalt road between Zvornik and the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, I passed by a truck belonging to the Zvornik Brigade with soldiers coming back from Snagovo. Now, within the compound of the barracks, in front of the building, I happened to meet Colonel Vasic, the chief of the Zvornik security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were walking along together, I said hello to him and we had a chat. He was interested in a policeman of theirs that had been captured the night before, Captain Zoran Jankovic, who was captured at Snagovo and as we were walking along we entered the headquarters, the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of us went up the staircase, up to the first floor from ground floor level, and Major Dragan Jokic, from the corridor on the right-hand side on the ground floor called out to me. So I went back down to the ground floor and Vasic - Colonel Vasic - went up towards our offices up there. So I briefly spoke to Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to be clear: This is the morning of what day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th, around 11.00, a little after 11.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called me. He said: Major, just a moment. I went back. And he said he had a lot of problems with securing the prisoners of war and with burying them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he say anything else that you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him who he had informed about this state of affairs, and he said that Beara, Popovic, and Nikolic were taking people wherever they felt like it and however they felt like doing, and that Colonel Popovic had ordered that nothing should be conveyed through radio communication about the prisoners and that nothing should be recorded, written down, in that connection either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do when he told you this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was none of my business, and I made a gesture with my hand, refuting this, and they told me from the command that the commander would be there shortly. So I went up the staircase again to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you tell him it was none of your business?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through impotence maybe. It wasn't a suitable response at all events, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this operation your business?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you make any sort of physical gesture to Mr. Jokic when you made the statement about it being none of your business?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's asked and answered. He described his gesture. He made already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think Mr. McCloskey has asked what kind of gestures the witness made. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, can you describe what kind of gesture you made? Can you just show us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I waved my hand and went up the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just like you just did, just sort of taking your right hand and moving it --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Jokic say anything else as you went up the staircase?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, he said that from the corps command they had reported that the commander would be arriving shortly, at any moment, and I left, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went up the stairs, down the corridor, the hallway on the first floor of the command headquarters, to my own office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there anybody at that office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front, in the ante-room. And if I can put it that way, there was Colonel Vasic waiting, and the two of us entered my office together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe -- before I get there: Do you know if there was -- when you and Mr. Jokic had your exchange, do you know if there was anybody else that was within hearing distance of that exchange?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nobody. At least, I didn't see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you describe the meeting you had with Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in my office -- actually, the two of us went into my office together. We sat down. Our conversation started in the following way: We discussed that Captain Jankovic, Zoran Jankovic, the policeman who had been captured, and the strength of the column itself. And I don't think that Colonel Vasic himself believed that there were so many men in the 28th Division, that it was such a strong column. And so briefly after hearing from me, he asked me whether I had seen so many people with my very own eyes, so many men. And when I said that I really had, and told him about it, he suggested that the best thing to do would be to allow the column to go through. From late at night on the 14th, as the Muslims from the 28th Division column had arrested this man Jankovic, they had already called up on the radio and asked us to let them through. So the two of us discussed this and we thought that the column should be allowed to pass through. Vasic told me of some experience he had gained during 1992. Of course, all this was very fast. It wasn't an actual conference and discussion, but he said he had been surrounded at Konjuh or somewhere like that and he thought that the Muslims would fight to the death, and that the best thing we could do was allow them to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remember to keep it slow. We need to keep the conversation slow. Was this police officer Jankovic eventually released by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I remember correctly. I think he was exchanged right after the war. I don't know exactly when, but he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And okay. What happened as this discussion is continuing? What else is discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the two of us talked. Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel Ljubomir Borovcanin walked into the office, and with him was the commander of this special police detachment from Sekovici. I don't know which rank he had. Milorad Stupar was his name. The two of them entered the office together and joined in our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Stupar, do you know, in rank or authority above or below Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasic, or Colonel Vasic, briefly spoke about the situation. As he had put it, this was a situation that Bratunac had been brought into without much thought. Before that, on the night of the 13th, a large number of prisoners had been brought in. There weren't enough people to guard them. And some of these groups remained on the buses. I remember that he said -- that he told a story that during the night these prisoners got restless and started shaking the buses, rocking the buses. So they had a lot of trouble pacifying them. In the meantime, as we were talking about this, we tried -- or rather, I tried to get approval from the Superior Command for opening a corridor and for allowing the column of the 28th Division to pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do to try to contact Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I called the command of the corps and I asked to speak to the commander of the brigade. However, they told me that he had set out in the direction of Zvornik. At the corps headquarters there weren't any other officers who I think could have issued the kind of approval or order that I had in mind T then I called the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and there I was put through to speak to Major General Miletic. I spoke to him briefly, and I told him in the briefest possible terms where the column was and what the dangers involved were. I told him the Zvornik would fall and that practically half of the Zvornik Brigade would be destroyed. He ordered me to use all the technical equipment available and that this column had to be destroyed. He objected. Why was I using this line that was not secure? And he slammed the phone. He simply disconnected the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you -- at the time, what did you think General Miletic's position was at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of the operations department. I don't know what it was called. But he was the operations man at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what the extension number was that he was speaking to you on, what extension you had to go through to get to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those few days he answered the phone when extension 155 was dialed. That's the switchboard at Panorama, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Panorama is the code-name for what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. McCloskey. Panorama is the code sign for the switchboard of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you able to speak directly to General Miletic from the phone in your office?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've already said that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just again describe to us: The phone in your office would go to where and how would that connection be made to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dialed the extension from my office and I called our switchboard, the one that was one floor above us, and a girl who was there answered the call, and I asked her to put Panorama through to me. And then it's their part of the job, the part of the job of the signalman. After a while the girl said to me: You've been put through. And the voice on the other end said: This is Panorama. And I asked to speak to one of the generals, and General Miletic then spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what did you do after this short conversation with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I was taken aback. I saw that there would be total failure. Colonel Vasic was sitting there, and I think that he made a joke. I personally think this was a joke, saying something like the army is stupid, whatever. Now we're going to ask for the approval from someone from MUP to let these troops through. And he called somebody in Pale. I think he referred to an advisor of the Ministry of the Interior. He was calling from the civilian phone. The speakerphones were on. And the person on the other end of the line - and I really can't remember who that was now, and I didn't even know the man - this person said, after Vasic spoke about this difficult situation, this person said that the column -- or rather, Vasic said that the column should be released, and this other man said: How did you ever get this idea? Call up the army, get the air force in, and destroy all of them. Then I was really taken aback, like everybody else in the office, I think. I personally came to the conclusion that our superiors really had no idea as to what was going on in respect of this column and what kind of a danger this constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What in particular was it that this assistant to the minister said that caused you to be so taken aback?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things. Firstly, to destroy this column. I mean, we really had no possibilities to do that, even if we wanted to do so. This was a force to reckon with. And secondly, that the army should engage the air force -- well, first of all, we were not at a level that could do that, and we had all known by then that UNPROFOR had imposed a no-fly zone, and we all knew that combat aircraft could not be engaged at all. And we were talking about minutes, not days. So this could not be discussed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the speakerphone on when you had your conversation with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I spoke to General Miletic through the switchboard, through that ordinary military phone, whereas Colonel Vasic talked from the civilian phone, and that is why the speakerphone was on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened then during this meeting? Was there anything else discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, as we were trying to make other contacts and as we were thinking who else we could call, I said, sort of more on my own: How did the corps command remain without anybody there? Where were the appropriate superiors? Where was General Zivanovic? Then Mr. Borovcanin said to me that the commander of the Drina Corps was General Krstic, or rather, that Zivanovic was no longer commander, and that's when I first found out that this replacement had taken place. I didn't know about it until then. In the meantime, in addition to what I've already said what Vasic said about what had happened on the previous evening in Bratunac and the problems that were there on the buses and things in connection with that, Colonel Borovcanin first wondered how come so many soldiers of the 28th Division could pass by. I had the impression that everybody thought that far less troops had passed by. He told me that they had blockaded that road from Konjevic Polje to Kravica and that there was a lot of fighting there and that there were quite a few casualties, and they had taken quite a few Muslim prisoners. Then he was upset. It was my understanding that he was expressing his dissatisfaction over the fact that the police - and when I say the police, I'm referring to his own civilian police - was used to escort these convoys of buses. And he said that he did not want the civilian police to guard prisoners when they arrive at their destinations. In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "he," who are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about Colonel Borovcanin. In the meantime, in the meantime, at one moment - I really don't know which rank he held. He did have a rank - Mr. Stupar addressed me and asked me whether I knew a certain person, an officer who they called Oficir, officer. This was a person in his unit who had graduated from some military school. And I said that I did not know such a man, and he told me that he got killed in Kravica. He explained this incident, as he referred to it, that over there they were either guarding prisoners or taking them from one facility to another in Kravica. And at one moment one of the Muslims who was being guarded there grabbed a rifle are, an automobile rifle, and killed this officer. The way he told it, the soldiers who had been there - policemen, that is - as he put it, out of revolt, killed these men who were guarded at the warehouse, the ones they were guarding there at the warehouse in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Stupar give you any indication of the numbers of Muslims that were killed in this warehouse in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This might be a good time to break, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Before that, would you please inform me how much time do you need until you finish your direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me just take a quick look at my notes. It's hard to say, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's hard to say. It may depend on how many other conversations we have during the testimony. But hopefully, an hour to two hours, probably an hour and a half to two hours. There are some documents that may take longer, but I hope not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the Defence team, you know, has been quiet for quite a long time and they are very cooperative, you have to understand. Well, we'll resume at 15 past 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, we ended the last session. We were at that meeting at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters where you were present with Mr. Vasic Mr. Borovcanin, and Mr. Stupar. At some point in that meeting, did someone arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After a while perhaps about 20 minutes later - excuse me - after I talked to General Krstic, Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you describe to us, before we get to Pandurevic, can you describe your contact with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we could not get approval beforehand from anyone to open this corridor so that the column could pass through it, Mr. Borovcanin told me that General Krstic was now commander, instead of Zivanovic. I then remembered to call the signal unit in the corps of -- in the command of the Drina Corps and to ask for Major Jevdjevic, who was the signalman, and I assumed he could establish a link for me with General Krstic. And that's what I did. I spoke briefly with Jevdjevic first and I told him that Zvornik was just about to fall, I said that the situation was critical and I asked him to somehow establish a link with General Krstic for me. And indeed, the line was not even interrupted. Very soon, I had General Krstic on the line. I said to him, briefly, that the situation was critical, that Zvornik would simply fall, and that more than half of the Zvornik Brigade would be destroyed. He asked me why I was so terrified. He obviously did not understand and he did not realise what was going on. Then he said that I should not worry at all, that Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic and Legenda would arrive any minute, and that's how we ended this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how long after that did your commander, Pandurevic, arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN OBRENOVIC [Resumed]
